key: Heaven and earth do not act from (the impulse of) any wish to be benevolent; they deal with all things as the dogs of grass are dealt with.
s: The chapter opens here, then says the same of the sages; Wang Bi, on chapter 5, reads it as heaven and earth following what is so of itself, making nothing, while things order themselves: earth grows no grass for beasts, yet beasts eat grass.
src: Wang Bi, Laozi zhu, chapter 5, zh.wikisource (the Huating Zhang edition), revision 2354026 (2024)

evidence.words: 天地任自然，無為無造，萬物自相治理，故不仁也。 … 地不為獸生芻，而獸食芻
evidence.gloss: Heaven and earth leave things to what is so of itself; they neither act nor make, and the ten thousand things order one another of themselves; therefore they are not benevolent. … Earth does not grow grass for the beasts, yet the beasts eat grass.

reason: The problem holds: the old plain sense restated the key verse (no wish to be benevolent, dogs of grass). Rewritten to rules 1 and 2: the plain sense now places the verse as the chapter’s opening, which then says the same of the sages, with no four-word run of the key verse and nothing leaning on Legge’s parenthesis. The reading keeps Wang Bi and his comment on 天地不仁，以萬物為芻狗 (his base line is the key verse’s line), shortened: following what is so of itself (任自然), making nothing (無造, from 無為無造), things ordering themselves (萬物自相治理), and the grass and beasts example (地不為獸生芻，而獸食芻).
